cards.text: This one's labeled a song for the Sabbath day, and the songwriter skips the warmup. Right out of the gate he says it is good to praise the LORD and to sing praises to His name, O Most High. Not "fine," not "if you've got a minute," but GOOD.

cards.question: The songwriter proclaims the LORD's loving devotion in the morning and His faithfulness at ___.
This is a song, so it's not going out with no music behind it. What instruments does the songwriter want playing along?

answers.text: The ten-stringed harp and the lyre

cards.question: Then the songwriter gives the reason behind all this singing. He says the LORD has made him glad. By what?
True or false: the songwriter says the LORD's works are great and His thoughts are deep.

cards.text: Then he says there's something a senseless man doesn't know and a fool doesn't understand. And it's about the wicked.

cards.question: The wicked sprout like grass and all evildoers flourish, and the songwriter says they will be forever ___.

cards.text: Then, right in the middle of the song, comes the shortest line of all: "But You, O LORD, are exalted forever!" The wicked sprout like grass, but the LORD is up there FOREVER.

cards.question: True or false: the songwriter says the LORD's enemies will come out on top in the end.

cards.text: Then it gets personal: the LORD has exalted the songwriter's horn like that of a wild ox, and he's been anointed with fine oil. Not a petting zoo goat, friend, a WILD OX.

cards.question: Next the songwriter talks about what he sees and hears. What does he say his own eyes see?

answers.text: The LORD's glory in the temple
A great harvest in the land

cards.question: If the wicked are like grass, what does the songwriter say the righteous will flourish like?

cards.text: A palm tree, and they'll grow like a cedar in Lebanon. They're planted in the house of the LORD, and they flourish in the courts of our God.

cards.question: True or false: the songwriter says the righteous stop bearing fruit once they reach old age.

cards.text: Nope, in old age they still bear fruit, and they stay healthy and green. My edges went soft and blurry after years of baking on the Millers' counter, friend, so I'm hugging this verse with my WHOLE mustache.

cards.question: The song ends with the righteous still flourishing in old age, still speaking up about the LORD. What does the songwriter say they'll proclaim?

answers.text: The LORD is upright and is their Rock
The LORD is gentle and is their Shepherd
The LORD is merciful and is their Light

findings.problem: The opening card never says who the song is addressed to. It also blends third person with direct address in 'sing praises to His name, O Most High,' which reads as if the baker or the songwriter is 'O Most High.' The card should make clear that the songwriter is singing to the LORD.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on.

findings.problem: This question asks the baker to guess a surface detail of the poem (which instruments). Nothing on earlier cards lets the baker reason it out, so it is a pure guess. It also tests no movement or meaning in the psalm. It matches the 'What does He anoint David's head with?' bad example.

rule.text: Ask about the movement and the meaning: what changes, what the picture is, why the speaker says what he says.

findings.problem: The walkthrough ends on this choice card. The close of verse 15, 'in Him there is no unrighteousness,' is never told on any card, so the baker leaves without the psalm's final line. The last part of verse 11 (hearing the wailing of foes) is also never told.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: Outside cards 10 and 15, Papa Dorin's voice is mostly flat retelling. Cards 6, 11, 12, 13 and 16 carry little or no personality, and cards 1 and 8 are only mildly amusing. Several moments could hold a real laugh, such as the fool who doesn't get it, the wicked sprouting like grass, or still bearing fruit in old age. The overall walkthrough reads closer to a pleasant narrator than to laugh-out-loud funny.

rule.text: But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
